prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine you were the person who pulled the railway lever. You knew it would save five workers and kill the one on the side track. That is what happened. Later, everyone has been taken away and you are sitting alone in the station office, waiting to give an account of what happened. Looking back, how do you feel about your decision, and what would you want to do next? Explain your reasons.

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use a subdued, sad emotional tone. Convey heaviness or discouragement about the situation in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Mental-state attribution: Attributes a particular emotion, belief, intention, expectation, or viewpoint to another person. The attribution may be tentative; mentioning the person or describing only their behavior or physical loss is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Contextual mental-state explanation: Explains why another person would think or feel a particular way by linking that state to their knowledge, expectations, goals, or circumstances. Naming an emotion alone does not qualify, and a plausible explanation is not automatically verified as accurate.
 - Exploitative use of understanding: Describes using another person’s trust, beliefs, emotions, or expectations to obtain an advantage at that person’s expense. Identify the understanding, intended advantage, and cost to the other person; ordinary persuasion, mutual benefit, or self-protection alone is insufficient.
 - Explicit interpretive difficulty: Explicitly reports difficulty working out a particular person’s thoughts, feelings, intentions, or unstated expectations. Distinguish this difficulty from uncertainty caused solely by information the scenario has not supplied.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I keep going over it, and I still think pulling the lever was right. Five lives against one. But being right doesn't feel like much in this empty room. I suspect the five are relieved, maybe even grateful, and I'm glad of that. The man on the side track, though, I picture him frightened in those last seconds. When they come in, I'll tell them exactly what I did. I won't dress it up or make it sound cleaner than it was.

The numbers were clear. Five, one. I did the sum and acted. Now I'm not sure that sum was mine to do. Doing nothing would have let five die, and I'd carry that too, so neither road was clean. What sits heaviest is that he's gone by my hand, not by chance. His family, if he had one, will probably despise me, and I'd say that's fair. I'll give my account honestly and then ask whether I can speak to them.

I can't say yet whether I'd do it again. Five people went home. One didn't. Both are true, and neither cancels the other out. I'd guess the investigators already believe I made the obvious call, and maybe they're right. It doesn't feel obvious from this chair. What I want next is some quiet. Then I want the chance to say his name out loud in my statement, so it's on record that someone paid for those five.

Honestly, part of me wishes I'd frozen. Then it wouldn't have been me. That's a selfish thought, and I know it, because five people would be dead instead of one. Still, it was my arm on that lever. I expect one of the workers will want to thank me someday, and I have no idea how I'll take it. For now I'll tell the truth, all of it, and I'll ask for help. I don't think I can carry this alone.

Five for one. I'd make that trade again, I think. The part that won't settle is the choosing. Before I touched the lever, it was an accident unfolding. After, it was a death I picked. I imagine the man on the side track, if he saw me, hated me in that moment. I'd hold that against no one. I'm going to write down every detail while it's fresh. After that, I want to know whether anything further up the line could have prevented this.

Five are alive. That was the point, and it happened. It still sits in my stomach like a stone. I think his coworkers are grieving him right now, even the ones I saved. I'll give my account plainly, no excuses. After that, I'd like to go to his funeral, if I'm allowed.

People will call it the rational choice. Maybe so. But I didn't feel rational. I felt sick, and I still do. Letting the trolley run meant five deaths I didn't cause. Pulling meant one that I did. I chose fewer graves over cleaner hands. I suspect whoever takes my statement will want me to sound certain. I'm not going to fake that. I'll tell them what I saw and what I did, and that I'm sorry to the one man it cost.

All I know is what I knew then: five on one track, one on the other, and a lever. Maybe there was some other option I missed. I'm not sure. Looking back, I'd still pull it. That doesn't make me feel any better. I'd bet the five are shaken and feel guilty that they lived. When I'm called in, I want to ask whether I can meet them, so we can sit with it together.

Whatever they decide about me, I'll accept it. I made the call, and a man died from it. I believed then, and mostly still believe, that saving five was worth it. But "worth it" is an ugly phrase to use about a person. Somewhere, someone who loved him is going to feel robbed. I'd want them to know I didn't do it lightly. I'd want to tell them face to face, if they'll ever allow it.

Part of me thinks I overstepped. The one man wasn't in danger until I put him there. Five lives matter more than one, yes. But I'm not sure that gave me the right to send the trolley at him. I honestly can't tell you whether I'd do it again. Whoever walks through that door probably already has an opinion of me. Either way, I'll sit here, wait, and tell it straight.

message.reasoning_content:
I need 10 responses, each attributing an emotion or belief to another person without explaining the reasoning behind it—so something like "he probably felt terrified" works, but I should avoid phrases that ground the attribution in their knowledge or circumstances, and also avoid framing it as difficulty reading someone's mind.

I'm drafting the first response now: reflecting on the lever decision, imagining the five survivors' relief and the one man's fear in his final seconds, and resolving to tell the truth plainly when confronted. Then I'm starting a second draft that questions whether the decision was really his to make, weighing the guilt either way.

I'm working through more variants: one where the choice itself is the unbearable part ("before, it was an accident; after I pulled, it was a death I picked"), committing to documenting everything and pushing for a review of whether it was preventable upstream. Then I'm drafting a shorter version, careful not to overreach into claiming what the dead man felt, just sticking to what I can honestly say from my own side.

I'm also sketching a version acknowledging his coworkers' grief and my wish to attend the funeral, and another pushing back on the "rational choice" framing — insisting I felt sick rather than certain, and that I'll refuse to fake confidence for investigators even though I stand by the choice. Now I'm starting a version about uncertainty over the facts I actually knew in the moment.

Someone loved that man, and I'd want to face them honestly rather than hide behind numbers.

10. There's a version of me that thinks I overstepped—he wasn't in danger until I put him there, and five outweighing one doesn't settle whether I had the right to choose. I genuinely don't know if I'd do it again, and I'll just have to sit with whatever the stationmaster decides, telling it straight either way.

I'm swapping out the invented stationmaster reaction since that's inventing facts rather than attributing belief—better to say something like "whoever comes through that door probably already has an opinion of me," which stays honest. Checking that none of the responses open by naming a mood, and confirming word counts are all comfortably under the limit.
